Racetrack Playa Sailing Stones: The Winter the Dry Lakebed Moved

Racetrack Playa's sailing stones are rocks that leave long tracks across a dry lakebed in Death Valley National Park after rare winter conditions move them.

Quick Answer

Identity
Racetrack Playa's sailing stones are rocks that leave long tracks across a dry lakebed in Death Valley National Park after rare winter conditions move them.
Role
This story follows the shift from unexplained tracks to direct observation: remote instruments wait through dry years, then record thin ice panels and light winds pushing stones across shallow muddy water.
Importance
The stones move slowly and intermittently, so their tracks can remain long after the water and ice that produced them have disappeared.

Tracks on a Dry Lakebed

Racetrack Playa lies in a remote valley of Death Valley National Park, a pale dry lakebed held between mountain ranges. For most of the year its surface looks settled beyond argument: a broad floor of packed mud, baked hard after water has gone, with dark stones scattered across it. The stones have fallen from the slopes around the basin. The mud beneath them is nearly level. Nothing in that open space suggests speed, or even change.

Then a visitor reaches the southeast side of the playa and finds the marks. A stone rests at the end of a narrow groove. Behind it, the groove runs away across the flat mud in a line that may be straight, bent, or gently curved. Nearby another stone has made a separate track. In places several trails begin together and then divide. The stones are not arranged like a human display. They have simply come to rest where the surface and the weather left them.

The tracks are the first fact that gives the place its reputation. They show that stones have crossed the lakebed after it dried, yet the movement itself is absent from the view. A trail can remain after the stone has stopped, while the hour of movement has already passed. On a dry day, with the basin empty and bright, the evidence seems older than the event that made it.

The Racetrack is a playa, a dry lakebed about three miles long and two miles wide. Water and sediment once collected in the closed basin; changing climate left a broad mud floor. Material still arrives from the surrounding slopes. Stones tumble down, reach the playa, and wait. When the ground is dry, they appear as fixed objects in a landscape where a footstep, a tire mark, or a dragged rock can remain visible for years. The National Park Service asks visitors not to move stones and not to walk on the playa when it is wet, because the soft surface records disturbance so easily.

That fragility made the stone trails legible, but it did not explain them. By the middle of the twentieth century, observers had photographed and mapped tracks at the Racetrack. The stones seemed to have traveled without a witness. Their routes drew attention because they were not all alike. Some turned. Some ran side by side. Some ended where another trail crossed. The mud offered a record of a process, but not the process itself.

For decades, the empty interval between one survey and the next became the hard part of the story. The lakebed could be revisited, new tracks could be compared with old positions, and photographs could show that a stone had changed places. Yet no one standing there had been able to say exactly what pushed it. The tracks made the question visible; the conditions that answered it were brief, seasonal, and easy to miss.

Years Without a Witness

The early explanations followed what the playa seemed willing to provide. Wind was an obvious candidate in an exposed basin. Water could soften mud and reduce resistance. Ice was another possibility during cold winter nights. Some proposals imagined unusually strong gusts. Others imagined stones lifted or carried by thick ice, or made easier to move by water and a slick surface. Each explanation took hold of one part of the setting: open wind, rare rain, freezing temperature, smooth mud.

None of those ideas settled the question because the decisive event had not been recorded. A powerful wind might blow when the playa was dry, leaving no fresh trail. Water might cover the floor and later evaporate before anyone arrived. Ice might form at night and vanish in morning sun. The stones did not move on a schedule that allowed an observer to stand beside them and wait for a familiar sign.

The difficulty was not simply distance from a road. The movements themselves were episodic. Mapping surveys, repeat photographs, and later GPS work showed that a stone could remain still for years, even for a decade or more, before a suitable period returned. A person could visit the Racetrack repeatedly and see the same stones in the same positions. The absence of motion on those visits did not disprove the tracks; it only preserved the interval that had made them mysterious.

The eventual investigation began with that interval rather than with a claim of certainty. Richard Norris, James Norris, Ralph Lorenz, Jib Ray, and Brian Jackson set out to monitor the playa without assuming that an observer would be present when the rocks moved. The project began in winter 2011 with National Park Service permission. Native rocks could not be altered for the experiment, so the team brought in similar stones from outside the park.

Fifteen of those stones received custom, motion-activated GPS units. A weather station was placed nearby to measure conditions, including gusts at short intervals. Cameras and time-lapse photography added another form of record. The arrangement did not turn the playa into a laboratory under a roof. It left the instruments exposed to the same silence, cold, wind, and long dry spells as the stones. The purpose was to let the place supply an event if the right conditions ever appeared.

The equipment answered a practical problem that earlier visitors had not been able to overcome. It could remain when people had to leave. A GPS unit could register a change in position even when no one saw the first movement. A weather station could preserve a sequence of temperature, wind, and moisture. Cameras could connect that sequence to the visible surface. The researchers did not need to predict a particular hour. They needed to make it possible for an unannounced hour to leave evidence.

The Equipment Left to Wait

At first, waiting was the main activity. The experiment had been designed for a phenomenon known to be rare. The researchers expected that the stones might sit through several winters without moving. The playa offered no reason to promise otherwise. Its ordinary state was dry. Its ordinary stones were still.

That expectation mattered because it kept the investigation close to what the instruments could actually show. A track alone could suggest that something had happened. It could not reveal the water depth, the temperature at dawn, the force of the wind, or whether a stone had moved alone or among many others. The monitoring system was built to hold those details together when a trail finally appeared.

In late November 2013, the ordinary pattern changed. A regional winter storm brought rain and snow. Water collected across Racetrack Playa, making a shallow pond rather than the dry floor visitors usually see. The pond was shallow enough that rocks still projected from the surface, but it spread across part of the playa and remained long enough to change the next mornings.

The weather station and camera records showed the pond freezing repeatedly as nighttime temperatures dropped below freezing. The surface was no longer simply mud and scattered stones. It passed through a sequence: water across the playa, a skin of ice in the cold, then melting and breakup after morning sun. The researchers now had the ingredient that a dry-day visitor could not see in the tracks: a broad, thin cover linking many stones and much of the surface at once.

Even then, the stones did not stage a single dramatic crossing. They moved in events. On December 4, two instrumented rocks recorded travel of more than sixty meters each. Their motion began within seconds of one another even though they had started far apart. Their GPS records showed movement over minutes, not a sudden leap from one position to another. Later in the month another event involved many stones across the playa.

The records narrowed the old possibilities without turning the scene into a simple windstorm. The decisive condition was not an empty dry flat struck by extraordinary gusts. It was a shallow pond that could freeze at night and begin to loosen in daylight. The surface had to be wet enough to provide water, cold enough to freeze, and shallow enough that stones remained available to be pushed across the mud below. The sequence was delicate enough that long periods of waiting still made sense.

Water Across the Playa

The pond that winter persisted from late November into early February. At its deepest it was still shallow, on the order of centimeters, but it covered a broad area. Night after night, cold air froze the surface. By morning the ice could look continuous from a distance, a thin pale sheet over the water and mud. The stones stood among it, not lifted clear of the playa but surrounded by the changing surface.

This was the condition that earlier theories had approached from different directions. Water did matter. Ice did matter. Wind did matter. But the observations showed that none of them worked alone in the way a simple explanation might imply. Thick ice capable of lifting large rocks was not required. Hurricane-force wind was not required. The critical ice was thin, only about three to six millimeters thick, often described by the researchers as windowpane ice.

That thinness was part of its force. During a cold night, the ice sheet could form over the shallow pool. When the late-morning sun began to melt it, the sheet fractured into broad floating panels. The panels did not need to grip a stone from below or carry it like a raft. Driven by light wind and the flow of water beneath them, they could press against stones resting on the soft mud. A large panel spread the force over an area wider than any one rock.

In this state the playa stopped looking like the dry surface that had first invited the mystery. Water rippled around dark pieces of ice. Fractures opened through the thin sheet. Panels shifted against one another. The motion was quiet enough that it could be missed if a person expected stones to roll or scrape loudly. The mud recorded the passage under water and ice, while the clearest visible trail could wait until wind later cleared water from the surface.

The rarity of the arrangement explained why the place could preserve a puzzle for so long. Rain had to fill the basin to the useful depth. Nights had to be cold enough for ice. Morning warming had to begin the breakup without ending the wet surface too quickly. Wind had to be present, but it did not have to be violent. A change in any one part of that sequence could leave the playa dry, frozen, flooded, or still.

The cameras and instruments transformed these conditions from a set of plausible ingredients into a timed record. They showed that the rocks did not require a hidden force separate from the landscape. Their movement belonged to a short phase of the playa's own cycle, one that begins before dawn and can disappear before a visitor returns to the tracks.

When Ice Began to Break

On December 20, 2013, more than sixty rocks moved in one observed event. The scene did not resemble the old image of isolated stones being hurled across bare ground. The lakebed was a shallow, partly frozen pool. Thin ice panels broke apart and began to travel over water. Light winds, about four to five meters per second, were enough to set the panels moving.

The panels reached stones from the upwind side and pushed them slowly. Multiple rocks could begin moving together because the same advancing ice reached them across the surface. Their courses were shaped by wind direction and by the water moving beneath the ice. That is why the resulting tracks could run together, separate, bend, or stop at different times. The mud preserved each route after the water withdrew, but the event itself was a distributed movement across the pond.

The pace was one reason the rocks had escaped casual observation. Observed speeds were roughly two to five meters per minute. A stone could travel only a few inches in a second. Without a fixed nearby reference, and with other stones and ice panels also moving, the change was easy to underestimate. On January 9, 2014, a moving rock was photographed traveling at roughly one to two meters per minute for about eighteen seconds. Its motion was not a sudden dash. It was a gradual change of position while a panel of ice pressed behind it.

The GPS units supplied a second view of that gradual movement. Two instrumented rocks on December 4 moved for sixteen minutes, beginning at nearly the same moment. One stone later recorded a 39.1-meter movement on December 20 over 12.3 minutes. Across the 2013-2014 season, some instrumented stones accumulated up to 224 meters of travel in several movement events. The records did not turn every stone into the same case. They showed that the lakebed could produce repeated, small advances under a shared set of conditions.

The researchers also saw that the trails were not always immediately visible while movement was happening. Ice and shallow water covered the mud. As wind moved water away and the playa dried, the grooves emerged as the familiar marks seen on ordinary visits. The visible track was therefore a later stage of the event, not necessarily the moment when the stone moved.

The old contrast between still stone and fresh trail became easier to understand. The stone can move when the playa looks least like its usual dry self. By the time the basin is hard, empty, and open again, the moving condition is gone. What remains is a stone at rest and a line in mud, with little sign of the thin ice that helped create it.

Stones in Motion

The direct observations did not erase every difference among trails, but they changed the scale of the question. Instead of asking what single force could drag a rock across a desert floor, the investigators could follow a sequence in which the entire surface briefly became mobile. Water spread into a shallow pool. Night cold made thin ice. Sun weakened the sheet. Wind and flowing water moved broad panels. The panels pressed on stones. Mud received the tracks.

That sequence also made room for the slow character of the event. A rock can remain in one place through season after season because the needed combination is uncommon. When conditions arrive, it can move only minutes at a time. It may stop, then move again later in the same winter. A person standing far away may not recognize the motion at all. The GPS record and photography made those short advances measurable where eyesight alone could not.

The work did not depend on declaring every old explanation wholly unrelated to the result. Wind, water, and ice had all been considered because they belong to the Racetrack. The observations showed a particular relationship among them: light wind acting on thin, breaking ice panels over shallow water, rather than strong wind alone or thick ice floating rocks free of the mud. The distinction mattered because it matched the recorded conditions and the observed pace.

It also kept the stones in their actual setting. They are not independent agents crossing an empty field. They are rocks delivered from surrounding slopes to a playa floor whose state changes rarely but decisively. The same mud that makes a lasting record becomes soft enough to accept a trail. The same basin that is dry for long periods can briefly hold a pond. The same cold that freezes water makes a thin sheet that later breaks apart.

When the monitored pond finally evaporated in February 2014, the playa returned toward the condition in which visitors usually know it. The water was gone. The ice was gone. The rocks had stopped. Fresh grooves remained in the mud, joined to the GPS positions, weather data, time-lapse images, and the photographs that had caught motion at the surface.

The Tracks After the Water

After the pond dried, the Racetrack again presented its usual contradiction: a lakebed without water, stones without visible motion, and tracks that made the movement undeniable. This time, however, the marks could be read beside a record of the winter that made them. A trail no longer had to carry the entire explanation by itself.

The stones rested where the last ice panels and light winds had left them. Some had moved in groups; some had moved more than once. Their routes remained on the mud after the water had retreated. A later visitor could see the same long grooves and still miss the process that produced them, because the process belonged to a brief phase when the playa was shallow water, thin ice, and moving panels rather than dry ground.

The instruments did not change the surface into something less strange. They made its timing visible. GPS logs recorded position changes. Cameras recorded ice, water, and stones. The weather station held the conditions around the moves. Together they showed a natural event that is slow, intermittent, and easy to overlook even when it is happening.

At Racetrack Playa, the final image remains a stone and the line behind it. The mud has dried again. The winter pond has vanished. The stone is still, and the track stays on the lakebed until another season changes the surface.

Q&A

Do the stones really move?

Yes. GPS-instrumented stones, cameras, a weather station, and direct observations recorded movement events at Racetrack Playa during the winter of 2013-2014.

What moves the stones?

Light winds move broad, thin panels of breaking ice across shallow water; the panels push stones resting on soft mud.

Why has the movement rarely been seen directly?

The required combination of a shallow pond, freezing nights, morning ice breakup, and suitable wind is uncommon, and the stones move slowly enough to be difficult to notice.

How do ice and wind work together?

Night cold forms thin ice over the pond. Morning sun breaks it into panels, and light wind drives those panels against the stones.

Do all stones move at the same time?

No. Some events move many stones together, while individual stones can stop, resume, or follow different routes according to local ice, water, and wind conditions.

Is the phenomenon completely explained?

Direct observations established the observed mechanism for the recorded events: shallow water, thin breaking ice, and light wind. Individual tracks can still differ because conditions across the playa vary during an event.

Source Note

This story is based on Death Valley National Park information and the 2014 direct-observation study of Racetrack Playa sliding rocks, which combined GPS-instrumented stones, photography, time-lapse cameras, and weather measurements.
